title: “YOUR NAVEL IS A ROUNDED BOWL”—WAIT… WHY IS THE BIBLE TALKING ABOUT THE HUMAN BODY LIKE THIS?
paragraphs: “YOUR NAVEL IS A ROUNDED BOWL”—WAIT… WHY IS THE BIBLE TALKING ABOUT THE HUMAN BODY LIKE THIS?

The shocking intimacy of Song of Songs 7:1–3, the Hebrew poetry most Christians have never understood, and the beautiful truth about desire, dignity, shame, and the God who created the human body without embarrassment.
There are verses in the Bible that make you close your eyes and worship.
There are verses that make you fall to your knees and repent.
And then there are verses that make you stop reading, look at the page again, and whisper…
“Wait. Did God really allow THAT to be written in Scripture?”
This is one of them.
“Thy navel is like a round goblet, which wanteth not liquor: thy belly is like an heap of wheat set about with lilies.”
— Song of Solomon 7:2, KJV
Your navel?
A rounded goblet?
Your belly like a heap of wheat?
And just a verse later, the poet describes a woman's breasts as two young gazelles.
In the Bible.
The same Bible that commands holiness. The same Bible that warns against sexual immorality. The same Bible that calls believers to flee lust and glorify God with their bodies.
So what is happening here?
Is this a contradiction?
Is the Bible being provocative?
Or have generations of Christians become so uncomfortable with the human body that we have forgotten something profoundly beautiful about the God who created it?
Stay with me, because the answer reaches much deeper than ancient romantic poetry.
It reaches into the shame some people carry when they look in the mirror.
Into marriages where affection has slowly disappeared.
Into the hearts of believers who have confused holiness with embarrassment.
And into one of the earliest scenes in Scripture, where two human beings stood before God without clothing, without shame, and without fear.
But to understand why this passage matters, we must first allow the Bible to speak in its own language, within its own context, without forcing it to say something it never intended.
Because Scripture does not need us to make it less human to make it holy.
And the truth waiting inside this passage might change the way you see your body, your marriage, your struggles, and even the grace of Jesus Christ.
The Hebrew text of Song of Songs 7:2, corresponding to 7:3 in the Hebrew verse numbering, begins with these words:
שָׁרְרֵךְ אַגַּן הַסַּהַר אַל־יֶחְסַר הַמָּזֶג
Shorerekh aggan hassahar, al-yechsar hammazeg.
A close translation is:
“Your navel is a rounded bowl; may the mixed wine never be lacking.”
The Hebrew word שָׁרְרֵךְ (shorerekh) is traditionally understood as “your navel,” although some interpreters suggest that the image may refer more broadly to the woman's lower abdomen.
אַגַּן (aggan) means a basin or bowl.
הַסַּהַר (hassahar) describes its rounded form.
And הַמָּזֶג (hammazeg) refers to mixed wine.
The King James Version's phrase “which wanteth not liquor” uses older English in which “liquor” can mean a liquid or drink. The Hebrew specifically points to mixed wine.
Notice what the poet is doing.
He is not writing an anatomy textbook.
He is not delivering medical information.
And he is certainly not providing permission to treat a woman's body as an object for public consumption.
He is using the language of abundance, beauty, delight, and intimate admiration.
The imagery is deliberately sensual.
That is important to acknowledge.
We do not honor Scripture by pretending that sensual language is not sensual.
The Song of Songs is love poetry, and its celebration of physical attraction is part of its meaning.
But sensuality and sin are not identical.
That distinction matters more than many Christians realize.
Because somewhere along the way, some believers absorbed the idea that the human body itself was something suspicious.
That attraction was automatically dirty.
That married couples should be embarrassed by their own affection.
That the safest way to be spiritual was to become uncomfortable with anything physical.
But the Bible begins somewhere very different.
Genesis 1:27 tells us that God created humanity in His image, male and female.
And after surveying His creation, including embodied human life, God declared it “very good” (Genesis 1:31).
The Hebrew expression is:
טוֹב מְאֹד (tov me'od)
“Very good.”
Not merely tolerable.
Not an unfortunate physical shell imprisoning a supposedly more important soul.
Very good.
Then Genesis 2:25 records something extraordinary:
“And they were both naked, the man and his wife, and were not ashamed.”
Read that again.
Before the fall, there was nakedness.
But there was no shame.
There was embodiment.
But no humiliation.
There was marital union.
But no exploitation.
The human body did not become evil when humanity sinned.
What changed was the human relationship with God, with one another, and with ourselves.
After disobedience, Adam and Eve became aware of their nakedness in a new way, covered themselves, and hid from God (Genesis 3:7–10).
Shame entered the story.
Fear entered the story.
Hiding entered the story.
And humanity has been hiding ever since.
Some people hide behind expensive clothes.
Some behind carefully edited photographs.
Some behind religious language.
Some behind a marriage that looks beautiful in public but has grown painfully distant in private.
Some hide because another person taught them to despise their bodies.
And some carry shame because they have used their bodies in ways they now deeply regret.
Perhaps that is why this ancient poem can feel so unsettling.
It speaks openly about physical beauty in a world where bodies have become battlegrounds.
But we must be careful.
Song of Songs 7 is not a command for everyone to look a certain way.
It is not God's universal beauty standard.
It is not a checklist for evaluating a woman's worth.
It is the language of a particular lover delighting in a particular beloved.
And that makes the context essential.
The passage begins:
“How beautiful are thy feet with shoes, O prince's daughter! the joints of thy thighs are like jewels, the work of the hands of a cunning workman.”
— Song of Solomon 7:1, KJV
The Hebrew begins:
מַה־יָּפוּ פְעָמַיִךְ בַּנְּעָלִים בַּת־נָדִיב
Mah-yafu fe'amayikh banne'alim, bat-nadiv.
“How beautiful are your steps in sandals, O noble daughter!”
The expression translated “prince's daughter” or “noble daughter” is poetic language of honor.
The speaker is not beginning with contempt.
He is not humiliating the woman.
He is celebrating her.
Then comes the description of her body, moving through images of crafted jewels, a rounded bowl, wheat, lilies, and young gazelles.
In Hebrew poetic tradition, this kind of descriptive praise is often called a wasf, a poem celebrating the beloved's beauty through a sequence of images.
Its metaphors are not intended to be read as literal comparisons of physical measurements.
A belly is not literally a pile of grain.
Breasts are not literally animals.
A navel is not literally a wine vessel.
The images evoke beauty, vitality, softness, abundance, elegance, and delight.

When Song of Songs 7:2 describes the belly as wheat surrounded by lilies, the poet is drawing upon images of fertility, nourishment, and loveliness from the agricultural world familiar to his audience.
And when verse 3 says:
“Thy two breasts are like two young roes that are twins.”
— Song of Solomon 7:3, KJV
The imagery suggests graceful symmetry and tenderness.
This is the vocabulary of ancient love poetry.
And yes, it is intimate.
But here is something worth noticing.
The woman in Song of Songs is not merely a silent body being described.
Throughout the book, she speaks.
She desires.
She remembers.
She invites.
She expresses longing.
She celebrates her beloved.
In Song of Songs 7:10, she declares:
“I am my beloved's, and his desire is toward me.”
This is not a picture of one person possessing another like property.
The Song portrays mutual attraction, affection, and delight.
And that mutuality is part of what makes the book so remarkable.
In a world where human bodies are frequently reduced to commodities, Scripture gives us a poetic portrait in which love involves personal recognition and reciprocal desire.
The beloved is not merely a body.
She is a person.
And the body being celebrated belongs to someone who has a voice.
That is a distinction our generation desperately needs to recover.
Because there is a difference between being admired and being consumed.
There is a difference between being cherished and being used.
There is a difference between desire that honors another person and desire that treats another person as disposable.
Jesus makes that moral distinction unmistakably clear.
In Matthew 5:28, He warns against looking at another person with lustful intent.
The Greek expression includes:
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν
Pros to epithymēsai autēn.
“To desire her,” within the context of Jesus' warning about an adulterous intention of the heart.
The verb ἐπιθυμέω (epithymeō) can refer to desire or longing; context determines whether that desire is sinful.
Jesus is not declaring that every recognition of beauty is adultery.
He is confronting the deliberate cultivation of wrongful sexual desire.
The Song celebrates intimate delight.
Jesus condemns lustful intent.
These teachings are not enemies.
They address different moral realities.
The Bible can celebrate marital love while condemning adultery, exploitation, and sexual immorality.
In fact, it must do both to remain faithful to its own teaching.
Hebrews 13:4 says:
“Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.”
The same God who commands sexual purity also honors marriage.
The same God who forbids adultery also permits and celebrates faithful marital intimacy.
Holiness is not hatred of the body.
Holiness is the consecration of our entire lives, including our bodies, to God.
And perhaps this is where the passage becomes uncomfortably personal.
Because the question is no longer simply, “Why would the Bible describe a woman's navel?”
The question becomes:
What has happened to our understanding of the body that makes us more comfortable with shame than with God's original declaration of goodness?
Think about the person who avoids mirrors because years of criticism have convinced them they are unattractive.
The wife who wonders whether her husband still sees her after years of childbirth, exhaustion, and changing seasons.
The husband who has quietly come to believe that his worth is measured only by performance, strength, or physical appearance.
The young believer who wants to honor Christ but has never been taught how to distinguish healthy attraction from sinful lust.
The person who was violated, exploited, or shamed and now struggles to believe that their body still deserves dignity.
Song of Songs does not solve all these wounds.
And we should never pretend that one poetic passage can erase the consequences of trauma, betrayal, or abuse.
But it challenges the lie that the human body is inherently disgraceful.
Your body is not worthless because it has changed.
Your dignity is not erased because someone mistreated you.
Your value is not determined by whether another human being finds you attractive.
And your worth before God is not measured by how closely you resemble the woman described in an ancient love poem.
That woman is being celebrated within a particular relationship.
She is not being established as the standard by which all women must be judged.
The Christian understanding of human dignity begins much deeper than appearance.
It begins with creation in God's image.
And it finds its fullest redemptive hope in Jesus Christ.
But there is another danger we must avoid.
We must not turn Song of Songs into something it is not.
Throughout Christian history, some interpreters have read the Song allegorically as portraying God's love for Israel or Christ's love for the Church.
Those readings have influenced centuries of Christian devotion.
And Scripture certainly uses marriage imagery elsewhere to describe God's covenant relationship with His people.
Ephesians 5:25, for example, commands husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the Church and gave Himself for her.
But Song of Songs 7:1–3 does not explicitly identify the woman's navel, belly, or breasts as symbols of particular spiritual doctrines.
We should not invent hidden meanings and present them as though the Hebrew text demands them.
The poem's immediate literary subject is human love.
That is not a problem to be solved.
It is part of the Bible's witness to God's good creation.
And within the wider Christian canon, this celebration of faithful love can lead us to reflect on the God who designed humanity for covenantal relationships, dignity, and holiness.
But the passage does not need to become a secret code about Jesus to have a rightful place in Christian Scripture.
Its beauty belongs to the story of creation.
And creation belongs to the God revealed through Jesus Christ.
Now consider something even more astonishing.
When the eternal Son of God entered our world, He did not merely appear to be human.
He became flesh.
John 1:14 declares:
“And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us.”
The Greek reads:
Καὶ ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο
Kai ho logos sarx egeneto.
“And the Word became flesh.”
The word σάρξ (sarx) means “flesh.”
Its meaning varies with context, but here John is making an extraordinary declaration about the incarnation.
The eternal Word truly entered human existence.
Jesus Christ took on genuine humanity.
He experienced hunger.
He experienced weariness.
He wept.
He suffered.
He bled.
He died.
And He rose bodily from the grave.
Christianity is not a religion that teaches us to escape the physical world because matter is inherently evil.
It proclaims that the Creator entered His creation to redeem sinners.
And the bodily resurrection of Jesus is central to that proclamation.
This is why the human body cannot simply be dismissed as something unworthy of God's concern.
First Corinthians 6:19–20 calls believers to honor God with their bodies.
Paul writes:
Notice the direction of the command.
Not despise your body.
Not worship your body.
Not use your body however you please.
Glorify God in your body.
That means our physical lives matter morally and spiritually.
How we treat others matters.
How we handle desire matters.
How we practice fidelity matters.
How we respond to temptation matters.
How we care for those whose bodies have been wounded matters.
And how we speak about ourselves matters, too.
There is a terrible irony in condemning the very body God created while simultaneously claiming to honor its Creator.
But there is an equally dangerous error in using God's good creation as an excuse for sinful behavior.
The Gospel rejects both extremes.
We do not need to be ashamed that God made us embodied creatures.
And we do not have permission to turn bodily desire into our god.
Jesus calls us to something better.
A life where grace does not excuse sin but transforms sinners.
A life where holiness is not merely a performance for religious people.
A life where repentance is possible because mercy is real.
A life where our bodies are not instruments of exploitation but are offered to God in worship.
Romans 12:1 urges believers to present their bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God.
That is an extraordinary invitation.
The same body you may have spent years criticizing can become an instrument of obedience.
The same hands that once participated in wrongdoing can now serve others.
The same lips that once spoke cruelty can now speak truth and encouragement.
The same life that once seemed dominated by shame can now become a testimony to grace.
Not because your past was harmless.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
But because Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose again.
And His grace is powerful enough to change the direction of a human life.
Perhaps someone reading this knows exactly what that means.
You have made choices you regret.
You have crossed boundaries you knew were wrong.
You have allowed lust to distort the way you look at people.
Or perhaps you were the one treated as an object, and someone else's sin left wounds you never deserved.
Those experiences are not morally identical.
The person who sinned needs repentance and forgiveness.
The person who was harmed needs safety, justice, compassionate care, and the assurance that another person's wrongdoing did not make them guilty.
But both need to know that Jesus Christ does not abandon people to darkness.
His mercy is not an invitation to continue in sin.
It is an invitation to come into the light.
First John 1:9 promises that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
And Romans 8:1 announces that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
That is not cheap reassurance.
That is Gospel truth.
Christ does not tell us that sin never mattered.
He went to the cross precisely because sin matters.
But He also declares that sin and shame do not have to write the final chapter for those who belong to Him.
That is not merely a beautiful phrase.
It is the story of what happens when human brokenness encounters the mercy of Jesus Christ.
The scandal of our rebellion.
The scandal of betrayal.
The scandal of hypocrisy.
The scandal of a world that can celebrate bodies while destroying the people who inhabit them.
And then, astonishingly, grace.
Grace that calls sinners to repentance.
Grace that restores what sin has disfigured.
Grace that teaches us to love without exploiting.
Grace that teaches us to honor without idolizing.
Grace that teaches us to live in our bodies without being enslaved by our desires.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the past never happened.
But by giving forgiven sinners a new future in Him.
And now, return to that opening verse.
“Thy navel is like a round goblet…”
Does it still sound strange?
Perhaps.
Ancient Hebrew poetry does not always resemble modern romantic language.
But perhaps it no longer sounds scandalous in the same way.
Because we can recognize what the poet is celebrating.
A beloved person.
Physical beauty.
Intimate affection.
The delight of love expressed through images of abundance and life.
And we can also recognize what the passage does not authorize.
It does not authorize lust.
It does not excuse infidelity.
It does not endorse objectification.
It does not make physical attractiveness the measure of human value.
And it does not promise that every person must marry or experience romantic desire to live a complete life.
Jesus Himself lived a fully human, holy, unmarried life.
And Paul honors singleness as a meaningful calling in 1 Corinthians 7.
So whether you are married, single, widowed, divorced, or walking through a difficult season, your dignity is not dependent upon romantic attention.
Your ultimate identity is not found in being someone's beloved.
For the Christian, the deepest security is found in belonging to Christ.
And that changes everything.
Because human admiration can fade.
Physical beauty changes with age.
Relationships can disappoint.
Even the most devoted spouse cannot carry the weight of being another person's savior.
But Jesus Christ remains faithful.
He does not love His people because they have perfect bodies.
He does not save them because they are attractive.
He does not forgive them because they have successfully hidden every embarrassing part of their lives.
He saves by grace through faith.
Ephesians 2:8–9 makes that clear.
Salvation is God's gift, not something we earn through moral achievement, physical appearance, religious performance, or financial generosity.
And that is why the Gospel is such astonishing news.
You cannot purchase the mercy of Jesus.
You cannot give enough money to make God owe you forgiveness.
Christ has already accomplished what no human payment could accomplish.
The question is whether you will turn to Him in repentance and faith.
And if you already belong to Him, whether you will allow His Word to reshape the way you think, love, speak, and live.
Maybe today that begins with repentance for the way you have looked at other people.
Maybe it begins with asking forgiveness from your spouse for years of emotional neglect.
Maybe it begins with refusing to keep measuring your worth against unrealistic standards.
Maybe it begins with seeking help for wounds you have carried in silence.
Or maybe it begins with opening your Bible again, this time without embarrassment, and allowing God to teach you what holiness actually means.
Because the Bible is not afraid of the human condition.
It speaks about love and longing.
Beauty and betrayal.
Marriage and singleness.
Desire and discipline.
Sin and forgiveness.
Death and resurrection.
And at the center of its redemptive message stands Jesus Christ.
Not a distant religious idea.
Not a motivational slogan.
The crucified and risen Savior.
The One who calls sinners out of darkness.
The One who receives the repentant.
The One who makes all things new.
Sit with the Scriptures.
Read Song of Songs 7 in its wider context.
Read Genesis 1–3.
Read Matthew 5.
Read 1 Corinthians 6.
Read John 1.
Ask yourself whether your understanding of holiness comes from God's Word or from fear, cultural assumptions, and teachings you have never examined.
And then, if you are willing, join this conversation.
Or perhaps your prayer is more personal.
You do not need to disclose private experiences publicly to participate.
A simple prayer or a verse that has encouraged you may be enough to strengthen someone else.
Someone may be quietly reading who needs to know that change is possible.
Someone may have spent years believing that being holy means hating themselves.
Someone may be trapped in lust and desperately needs to hear that repentance and freedom are possible through Christ.
Someone may be carrying shame for harm they never chose.
Your words, offered with wisdom and compassion, might point that person toward hope.
Not merely because the subject is surprising.
Not because an unusual Bible verse might attract attention.
Because people need to know that Scripture celebrates God's good creation without celebrating sin.
Because our generation needs something deeper than body worship on one side and body shame on the other.
We need Jesus Christ.

If someone comes to mind as you read this, consider tagging them respectfully, especially a friend who loves studying Scripture or someone who would appreciate a thoughtful discussion about faith and human dignity.
There may come a day when you need to revisit these passages, examine the Hebrew again, or remind yourself that God's Word is more beautiful and more challenging than the assumptions we bring to it.
Invite your family, your friends, believers who are struggling, those who have grown distant from their faith, and even seekers who are still asking difficult questions.
We are not here to pretend that following Jesus is easy.
We are here to keep pointing one another toward the Savior who is worthy of our lives.
And for those who want to help this ministry continue and grow, there is another meaningful opportunity.
Scripture teaches that giving should come from a willing heart, not pressure.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
These products can serve as everyday reminders of biblical truth and opportunities to share encouragement with others.
It is participating in a ministry effort that seeks to keep Scripture accessible, Christ central, and discipleship meaningful.
Read the Scriptures.
Use the free resources.
Pray for the ministry.
And continue growing in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.
Because the Gospel is not for sale.
And the worth of a soul is never measured by a monthly payment.
What matters is that Christ is proclaimed faithfully, people are encouraged to examine God's Word, and lives are transformed by His grace.
Now, before you leave, remember where this entire conversation began.
With a verse that seemed almost too intimate to belong in the Bible.
A navel described as a rounded bowl.
A belly compared to wheat surrounded by lilies.
A woman's beauty celebrated through the imagery of ancient love poetry.
What first appeared shocking became an invitation to examine something much deeper.
The goodness of creation.
The dignity of the human person.
The holiness of covenant love.
The danger of lust.
The tragedy of shame.
The necessity of repentance.
And the redeeming grace of Jesus Christ.
Perhaps the greatest surprise is not that the Bible speaks so openly about the human body.
Perhaps the greater surprise is that we have sometimes forgotten how deeply God cares about the whole human person.
He created us.
He knows our frailty.
He sees our sin.
He knows our wounds.
And He calls us to Himself through Jesus Christ.
Not so we can continue hiding.
But so we can walk in truth.
Not so we can excuse our darkness.
But so we can repent and receive His mercy.
Not so we can worship the body.
But so we can glorify the One who made us.
And if the Gospel has taught us anything, it is this:

The body you were taught to despise was created with dignity, the sin you were tempted to hide can be brought into the light, and the life you thought was beyond redemption can still be transformed by Jesus Christ.
